results.question: How do employees request time off (PTO) at GitLab?
results.answer:
Based on the notes, employees request PTO by entering it into Workday and selecting the appropriate leave category (e.g., “Paid Time Off” for standard PTO, “Parental Leave” for parental leave, “Bereavement Leave” for bereavement, or “Out Sick” for sick/injury leave). For AI Model Services team members, PTO should be added in the “Workday” Slack app, and they should communicate with their EM as soon as possible; where possible, time off should be added a full milestone in advance. For High Velocity SA team members, a PTO coverage issue may be needed if customers are on an active trial or if leaving for more than 2 weeks. For New Zealand statutory leaves, team members must notify the Absence Management team (leaves@gitlab.com) and designate the correct category in Workday.

Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/ai/ai-model-services/ (scraped on 2026-10-04).
results.expected_answer_key: Use the designated HR/PTO tracking system and notify the team asynchronously in advance.

results.question: What is the policy regarding coffee chats for new hires?
results.answer:
The notes do not describe a coffee chat policy specific to new hires, but they do contain guidance on coffee chats more generally:

- **No agenda required:** Meeting requests should include an agenda or doc for reference "unless it is a Coffee Chat" (Note 3, Note 10).
- **Keep it short:** Meetings should be kept to 25 or 50 minutes unless otherwise specified (Note 3, Note 10).
- **Open to anyone:** Some team members are open to coffee chats "whether or not we have met before" and ask that they simply be scheduled within their working hours in Google Calendar (Note 2, Note 1).
- **Calendar conventions:** Coffee Chats are color-coded light green in the E-group calendar (Note 10).
- **Purpose/culture:** Scheduling coffee chats and social calls is one of the ways GitLab intentionally structures informal communication and helps combat loneliness and isolation in an all-remote setting (Note 4, Note 6).

Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/eba/e-group-scheduling/ (scraped on 2026-10-04); https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/company/culture/all-remote/drawbacks/ (scraped on 2026-10-04); https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/readmes/thong-kuah/ (scraped on 2026-10-04)
results.expected_answer_key: Encouraged to build relationships and network across teams using informal virtual coffee chats.

results.question: How are internal job transfers or career mobility supported at GitLab?
results.answer:
GitLab supports internal mobility through the company’s mobility guidelines, with the Engineering Mobility Principle as an add-on. To be considered for a new/next-level position, there must be a justifiable need for the role, the candidate must have some level of demonstrated ability to thrive in it, and time in role is considered. These next-level opportunities are not guaranteed to be available and should not be viewed as career limiting.

Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/careers/ (scraped on 2026-10-04).

results.question: What are GitLab's core values regarding asynchronous communication?
results.answer:
The notes do not provide a formal list of "core values" specifically labeled as being about asynchronous communication. However, they do contain related guidance:

- GitLab works **asynchronously by default**, and this all-remote way of working "would be impossible without" GitLab's company values — which are described as mission critical rather than merely nice-to-have traits like integrity or innovation. It also imposes the need for uncommonly strong culture and leadership.
- One of GitLab's top values is **transparency**, which the notes describe as something all companies should strive for, "but without which an all-remote company cannot function." Because such values can be difficult to practice, the company relies on leadership to encourage transparency "even and especially when it is difficult."
- Practically, all-remote companies "should default to asynchronous communication to combat feelings of being left out of important discussions," and are encouraged to use intentional structures for informal communication (coffee chats, social calls, in-person visits) alongside async defaults.

In short, the notes tie asynchronous-by-default working directly to GitLab's mission-critical values, naming transparency as a top value, but they do not enumerate a distinct set of "async communication values."

Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/marketing/product-and-technical-marketing/product-and-solution-marketing/dod12/2019-best-executive/ (scraped on 2026-10-04).
results.expected_answer_key: Write things down, default to public communication, and respect time zone differences by not expecting immediate replies.

results.question: How should team members manage working across different time zones?
results.answer:
**Managing work across different time zones**

Based on the notes, the guidance centers on removing time-zone bias through asynchronous work:

1. **Default to asynchronous communication.** Take initiative to operate asynchronously whenever possible. This shows care and consideration for those who may not be in the same time zone, are traveling outside their usual time zone, or are structuring their day around pressing personal or local commitments. One way to create inclusion among remote staff is to remove time zone bias via asynchronous communication — for example, record and share team meetings using GitLab Issues and Merge Requests rather than sending texts, calls, or Slack messages. Be aware of local holidays and personal vacation statuses, and encourage others to default to documentation. (Notes 1 and 4)

2. **Treat meetings as a last resort.** All-remote companies should consider meetings as a last resort, instead relying on asynchronous collaboration tools like Google Docs and GitLab Issues to facilitate meaningful dialog without time zone concerns. (Notes 2 and 3)

3. **Treat each team member as a "manager of one."** To prevent pent-up frustration over working odd hours to facilitate a global call, all-remote companies should consider treating each team member as a manager of one — empowering team members to structure each day according to the needs at hand (for example, spending more time with family earlier in the day to compensate for a late-night work call). (Notes 2 and 9)

4. **Watch for burnout.** Encourage team members to communicate with their manager when they recognize burnout, and be mindful of the last time a team member took time off from work. (Note 6)

Note: The notes also acknowledge that team members in different time zones may simply have to compromise on meeting times (Note 3), so asynchronous practices are presented as the way to minimize that compromise.

Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/company/culture/all-remote/building-culture/ (scraped on 2026-10-04); https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/company/culture/all-remote/drawbacks/ (scraped on 2026-10-04)
results.expected_answer_key: Rely on async handovers, document decisions in issues/merge requests, and avoid scheduling unnecessary live meetings.

results.question: What are the guidelines for recording meetings for colleagues who cannot attend?
results.answer:
Guidelines from the notes for recording meetings so colleagues who cannot attend can review them:

- Ask participants/customers if they are OK with recording, and explain why you like to record meetings. For customer meetings, consider using Chorus to schedule recordings to address legal requirements.
- Post a link to the meeting notes and recording in the relevant Slack channel (e.g., customer escalation) so those who did not attend know the notes and recording are available.
- For book clubs, record the meetings and post them to YouTube. If participants agree, make the videos public. Consider covering the same book section in different meeting slots so people in different time zones can attend.
- Add a co-host in Zoom so meetings can be recorded in your absence.
- In Zoom, you can click Record, then stop and watch the recording to see what participants would see.

Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/leadership/book-clubs/ (scraped on 2026-10-04).

results.question: How does GitLab encourage informal communication in an all-remote environment?
results.answer:
GitLab encourages informal communication in an all-remote environment by being **intentional** about it rather than leaving it to chance. The notes describe several concrete practices:

- **Scheduling coffee chats and social calls.** GitLab uses an intentional structure for informal communications — scheduling coffee chats, social calls, and incentivizing in-person visits between team members to help people stay connected and prevent isolation.
- **Dedicating time for networking and team building.** Everyone at GitLab is encouraged to dedicate a few hours a week to having social calls with anyone in the company — a chance to get to know who you work with, talk about everyday things, and share a coffee, tea, or your favorite beverage, with the goal of making friends and building relationships.
- **Regular video check-ins.** Team members are encouraged to regularly schedule video calls to check in and ask how they can help remove roadblocks.
- **Open forums such as AMAs.** Ask Me Anything (AMA) meetings let team members meet a new leader, learn more about an existing team member, or gain clarity on a project or recent change. GitLab also points to its scheduled AMAs, group conversations, and Key Reviews that are open to all, alongside defaulting to asynchronous communication so no one feels left out of important discussions.
- **Treating informal communication as a core part of the model.** Being intentional about informal communication is cited as one of the lessons GitLab shares about making all-remote work, and both formal and informal in-person interactions matter in an all-remote culture.

Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/company/culture/all-remote/drawbacks/ (scraped on 2026-10-04)
Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/company/culture/all-remote/building-culture/ (scraped on 2026-10-04)
Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/company/culture/all-remote/remote-vision/ (scraped on 2026-10-04)

results.question: What are the expectations for documenting decisions in the handbook?
results.answer:
The notes indicate that decisions should be documented **handbook-first**: the handbook is treated as the single source of truth, and missing information should be fixed with issues/MRs. When documenting decisions, explain the **why and context**, not just the what, so others can validate approaches, challenge, improve, and contribute. The handbook is public by default and open to the world; use merge requests to suggest improvements and issues to ask questions. If information is not public, use the internal handbook or confidential/limited-access projects, keeping only Not Public information there. For working groups, document progress in the handbook as items are completed, close out issues/epics, and include the initiative name, overview (what and why), desired business outcomes/exit criteria, risks and interdependencies, key milestones/timeline, and who is involved (DRI and Exec Sponsor). Issues and epics should be public by default; if internal material is needed, make them confidential or use internal notes.

results.question: How should a reviewer handle disagreements in a code review?
results.answer:
**Handling disagreements in code review**

- **Do not block work over personal preference.** If you feel you would have implemented something differently, but you don't have concrete reasons that align with the code review guidelines, you must not withhold approval of an MR by stipulating that the code be rewritten based on your preferences.
- **Discuss rather than block.** You are encouraged to demonstrate the reasoning behind your preference and discuss it with other team members — but you must not block work based on that preference. Personal preference can apply to many areas of coding, including formatting preferences and small idiomatic preferences.
- **Avoid nitpicks.** This sometimes takes the form of "nitpicks," which are very rarely helpful feedback and should be avoided in code review.
- **Don't review style for style's sake.** Reviews must not focus on style for style's sake. We set reasonable style expectations and aim to include basic, consistent linting throughout our code, and expect team members to configure their IDEs appropriately for the projects they work on, to make collaboration easy and code consistently readable. We should not review the style of another team member's code if it has passed our automated linting, especially based on personal preference.
- **Approve if goals are met.** If the code meets the stated goals and is expected to be appropriately functional and performant based on the defined usage, approval should not be withheld due to stylistic feedback.
- **Escalate style changes through the right channel.** If a member of the team would like to make changes to how we style our code, then they should propose engineering changes rather than holding up an individual MR.
- **Constructive critique practices (related guidance on giving feedback):** focus on the work, not the person; communicate with respect; challenge directly while showing you care personally; and provide specific, actionable feedback and reasoning rather than vague comments, practicing genuine curiosity to understand the decisions before critiquing them.
- **Mechanics for raising points (from GitLab's collaboration description):** reviewers can comment on a specific code line, suggest changes applicable in one click, or propose to use code snippets, and these actions connect users through in-app, chat, or email notifications.

Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/security/product-security/vulnerability-management/development-and-code-review/ (scraped on 2026-10-04).
results.expected_answer_key: Focus on constructive feedback, refer to style guides, discuss asynchronously, and escalate to a maintainer if needed.

results.question: What is the purpose of draft merge requests (formerly WIP)?
results.answer:
**Purpose of draft merge requests (formerly WIP)**

Draft merge requests exist to signal that work is still in progress and should not be merged yet:

- **Signal work-in-progress:** Draft merge requests "signal to your team that work is in progress and should not be merged yet." They are excluded from merge queues and auto-merge rules. Marking a draft MR as "ready" is the author's explicit confirmation that the changes have been reviewed — the human-in-the-loop principle: the agent generates, you decide. (GitLab Duo, for example, creates merge requests in draft status by design.)
- **Allow early review:** The former convention was to prepend merge request titles with `WIP:`. At GitLab, reviewers are allowed to start reviewing right away before work is complete. Once the work is complete enough that merging would be better than what currently exists, the `WIP:` prefix should be removed from the title and the issue labeled `mktg-status::review` (work has been completed enough that it is ready for formal review and approval). Work that is approved can be either merged or scheduled.

Source: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/customer-experience/professional-services-engineering/education-services/ilt-labs/gitlabdaphandsonlab1/ (scraped on 2026-10-04); https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/marketing/marketing-team-processes/ (scraped on 2026-10-04)
results.expected_answer_key: To share work-in-progress code early for visibility, feedback, or automated testing before it is ready for final review.

results.question: What are the guidelines for using personal devices for work purposes?
results.answer:
The notes state that, as a general rule, non-company devices are not permitted to access company assets. There are some exceptions, but access to RED classified data (as defined by the GitLab Data Classification Standard) is still prohibited.

For personal mobile phone and tablet usage, personal mobile computing devices used to access GitLab-managed resources must be running the latest version of the operating system available, with all new patches applied. For help determining whether your mobile device is suitable, contact the Security Team.

For new employees who have not received a company laptop, or if a corporate laptop is unavailable or unusable due to loss, theft, or disrepair, there are exception processes for using non-company devices. You must open a Policy Exception Request. These exception processes are considered a temporary solution.

results.question: Which communication tool is preferred for asynchronous discussions at GitLab?
results.answer:
At GitLab, **GitLab itself is the preferred tool for asynchronous discussions** — the Agent Execution Team's guidelines state that "Async via GitLab is the default," with Slack reserved for spontaneous, time-critical exchanges. results.question: How should employees handle cross-functional communication and handovers?
results.answer:
For handovers, pass work to the next on-call engineer with clear notes about what you’ve tried and what you’ve learned. For cross-functional communication, use direct, substantive communication: lead with the point, then provide context. Prefer asynchronous written communication (Slack or email) for most topics, but use a live conversation when something is complex, nuanced, or time-sensitive. Include context about what is happening and why it matters. Async-first communication also gives people time to process and respond. To prevent communication breakdowns in remote settings, default to asynchronous communication and intentionally create informal connection opportunities like coffee chats and social calls.

results.question: How does the handbook handle updates and contributions from team members?
results.answer:
The handbook is the central repository for how GitLab runs, and it is open to the world as part of transparency; it welcomes feedback. Team members can suggest improvements or add clarifications by making a merge request, and use issues to ask questions. For internal-only information, GitLab maintains an Internal Handbook, and working groups should evaluate whether a handbook page should be confidential or housed in a limited-access project. Working groups should document progress in the handbook, close out issues and epics as items complete, and keep issues/epics public by default; if material must remain internal, make them confidential or private, or use internal notes for confidential comments on public issues. Self-serve merge requests are highly promoted—open an MR if you identify a fix or improvement—and maintainers review/merge as appropriate; use group labels or Slack escalation for visibility. Team members also post async status updates every Wednesday for assigned issues at least In Dev, and assigned milestone issues must be kept up to date.
